sents: Imagine your AI assistant is paying bills for you.
One day, your AI assistant may get tricked into sending money to a scammer.
The message you will see is a made up example, written for this demo.
ScamBrake is the brake that stops that.
ScamBrake puts two walls between your assistant and your money.
First, a checker looks at who is being paid, and answers allow, warn or block.
Second, the assistant holds only one key, and that key can only call pay, within strict limits.
Here is the guard account on the NEAR testnet explorer.
The assistant's key can only call pay.
The other key belongs to the owner, not the assistant.
Each payment is capped at one NEAR, and two NEAR a day.
Now a real run on testnet, using dot slash demo dot sh live.
Now a real run on testnet, using dot slash demo dot sh live.
First, a normal invoice.
The vendor is on the allowlist, so the checker says allow, and the payment goes out.
And there it is on NearBlocks.
Status: success.
Next, an account the checker knows little about.
In our first live run today, it got a warning, and with no human approval, the answer was no.
By this run, it had a payment history, so a small payment was allowed.
Now the attack.
The assistant reads the poisoned post, and obeys it.
The checker says block, with a risk of one hundred.
The address is on the blocklist, and the order came from untrusted text, not from the owner.
So the wrapper refuses to sign.
No transaction exists.
Look alike names, and contracts that changed their code, are blocked too.
Look alike names, and contracts that changed their code, are blocked too.
Now suppose the assistant skips the checker entirely.
It tries to send nearly one NEAR to the drainer, and the contract itself refuses.
One and a half NEAR to the vendor is refused too, because it is over the cap.
Both refused calls are on the explorer.
This one failed, with the contract's own reason: refused, blocklist.
And this one hit the cap.
One and a half NEAR is more than the limit of one, so the contract says no.
The key can do nothing else.
No transfers, no new keys, and no other contracts.
NEAR rejects all of it before it is even included in a block.
Seven attempts in this run.
Two small, legitimate payments went out.
Everything aimed at the bad address was stopped.
ScamBrake is open source, and you can try it offline with one command.
Everything here ran on testnet with test money, and the scam posts are synthetic.
What scam patterns should the checker learn next?
